utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case number IT-09-92-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Peter McCloskey, and with me is Dermot Groome, Roeland Bos, and Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Branko Lukic and Mr. Milos Saljic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Special word of welcome to you both because you have taken over duties now from duty counsel, as I understand, and Mr. Saljic, if I am well informed, is a legal consultant to the Defence of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first Status Conference in this case. And although I am sitting alone today, I inform the parties that a number of decisions that will be announced later have been taken by the Chamber as a whole. The purpose of this Status Conference is to start organising the pre-trial phase of this case, including setting dead-lines for when certain tasks should be completed. The Chamber will expect both parties' full commitment to efficient pre-trial proceedings. This also includes organising their support teams which will be needed since the parties will be expected, already from the beginning, to substantially contribute to the preparation of this case for trial. Mr. Mladic, I see you are touching your earphones. Can you hear me in an a language you understand or are there any difficulties?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am just trying to put my glasses on. I apologise. But I do hear you well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladic. Then I will wait a moment. Then we will proceed. At the outset, the Chamber notes that it is seized of a motion by the Prosecution, which was filed on the 16th of August to sever the indictment. The Defence is due to respond to this motion the 31st of August. Normally it would be the 30th, but that's a UN holiday; thus, it will be the 31st of August of this year. The Chamber's consideration of the motion does not prevent it, and also should not prevent the parties, from proceeding with the pre-trial planning in this case. And the Chamber's pre-trial plan includes, first, completion of disclosure by the Prosecution; then, dealing with any preliminary motions that the Defence will file; making decisions in relation to Rule 73 bis(D); the parties agreeing on facts that are not in dispute; dealing with any motion on judicial notice of adjudicated facts; the parties filing their pre-trial briefs; the Prosecution filing its Rule of 65 ter submissions; and the Prosecution start filing any motions pursuant to Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater. The Chamber will indicate dead-lines for some of these matters today. The Chamber is planning to hold monthly Status Conferences. During a 65 ter meeting, which was held last week, the Pre-trial Judge distributed a tentative schedule for Rule 65 ter meetings and Status Conferences to be held during the autumn of 2011 and to the beginning of 2012. The parties were asked to inform the legal officer of the Chamber within one week of any concern they had with this schedule. So, to the extent the parties have not done so already, would you please do so by the end of this day. An informal communication will be sufficient for this purpose. I will at a later stage explain to the parties how we will deal with informal communications as to how to put them on the record or sometimes how to file them, but sometimes e-mail exchanges, informal communications, assist in not losing time. The Chamber will issue a scheduling order in due course with regard to Rule 65 ter meetings and status conferences during the months to come. I move on to the next matter which is disclosure and preliminary motions. And I first would like to deal with Rule 66(A)(i) disclosure. But before we continue, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said, I will start with Rule 66(A)(i) disclosure. On the 12th of August the Defence filed a motion for you enlargement of the time to file preliminary motions. That motion sets out the procedural history, in particular with regard to the hand-over of disclosed material from duty counsel to permanent counsel. The Defence requests 25 days to file preliminary motions counting from the date of, and I quote, "full and appropriate compliance of Prosecution regarding disclosure of all supporting material." This matter was discussed at the Rule 65 ter meeting which was held on the 18th of August and the parties informed the Chamber then that full disclosure pursuant to Rule 66(A)(i) had taken place earlier on that same day. What then remains is for the Chamber to decide on the number of days the Defence has to file its preliminary motions counting from the 18th of August of this year. The Prosecution responded to the motion on the 23rd of August, 2011, and deferred to the Chamber's discretion with regard to the remedy sought. Having considered that a large part of the disclosure was made through the hand-over from duty counsel to permanent counsel already on the 8th of August 2011 but that the complete disclosure was made only on the 18th of August, the Chamber grants the Defence request. And the Chamber hereby instructs the Defence, to file its preliminary motions, if any, by the 12th of September, 2011. I move on to Rule 68 disclosure. As discussed during the Rule 65 ter meeting last week, if Chamber will also set a dead-line for the disclosure of Rule 68(i) material, that is exculpatory material. At the meeting I informed the Prosecution that the Chamber had November in mind, and the Prosecution was asked for their position on the dead-line and it stated that it would be in a position to provide the Chamber with that today. I therefore would like to invite the Prosecution to present its position in relation to a time-limit for Rule 68(i) disclosure. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have, of course, been looking studiously into this, and we had a very good meeting yesterday with Mr. Lukic where we have set out our intention to provide not only Rule 68 but all the relevant discovery materials in this case on a hard disk that he gave us, and that process will begin within the next few days. And we expect - for example the Srebrenica disclosure - witness statements, the complete file to be able to provided to Mr. Lukic within the amount of time it takes to transfer that, which is a day or two. The Karadzic-related materials that are basically the same as the current Karadzic case is -- will be a little more difficult because there is Rule 70 material laced in that. So providing the larger discovery material electronically we have to see if there is Rule 70 material that we first need to get clearance from, but in both those large discovery packages, which we intend to get to the Defence within a matter of days if -- without the Rule 70 problems, there is clear lists of Rule 68 material, and that should be - and I am just giving you my best estimate - at least the 90 per cent solution for Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could I interrupt you for a second. I specifically focussed on Rule 68(i) because the next item on my agenda would - and I will read that already to you so we can then return to 68(i), that the Chamber leaves to the parties to agree on law electronic disclosure is to be carried out technically in this case and, in this respect should the parties encounter problems, they are invited to address the Chamber as soon as possible. That's about, I would say, EDS disclosure, what remains after 68(i). The primary concern, and my question specifically was about Rule 68(i), exculpatory material, because the Chamber wants to avoid at a high cost that exculpatory material is not sought for systematically and that later on in the case that it emerges where we expect the Prosecution to systematically review their material on the existence of any exculpatory material. So that's where we mention specifically November. We suggested November and that's where I specifically asked your position on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. I understand, Mr. President, and the -- so my view is that 90 per cent of the identified Rule 68 material will be provided within a matter of, hopefully, days, and we are endeavouring and we have begun the process of a systematic review, a Mladic-specific systematic review, and Mr. Roeland Bos is in charge of and has begun to make that review as you have noted. And we have yet to be able to give you a -- have enough numbers and volume in mind to be able to give you a very accurate time-period by which that will be reviewed. We are realigning staff, we have realigned staff for this most crucial of jobs, and we will continue to do so. And we will endeavour to get this done by November. I certainly hope we can. We will intend, as we've, I think, mentioned, we would like to offer you information and reports on how we are doing so you can follow this process, but right now we have not yet been able to dig deeply enough into the material to give you an accurate idea of the number of documents that may be involved. It's clearly thousands, and we have got staff on this project and coming on this project, and we are hopeful that November will be something where we can give you an adequate assurance for that. So we are definitely trying, whether I can promise you that -- we can't promise that but we certainly can go for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am not seeking promises, I am seeking your position on a dead-line to be set by the Chamber. What I do understand is that you are explaining to me that you are doing your utmost best and that November is likely to be possible. This may guide the Chamber in setting a dead-line, because that's what we have on our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of your response, I will first discuss this briefly with my colleagues, but you should not be surprised if the Chamber would choose the 15th of November as the dead-line. Keep that already in the back of your mind. And, of course, whatever dead-line we set, and that is a systematic review of the existing material and any exculpatory material, that the obligation pursuant to Rule 68(i) is, of course, a continuing one, and that any exculpatory material the Prosecution would receive following the dead-line should be disclosed as soon as practical, as the rules tell you and us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I already dealt with the other Rule 68 disclosure. I do understand that the parties have had a fruitful meeting on that subject, and I only repeat we leave it, for the time being, in your hands, without setting specific dead-lines or giving any further guidance, but if there is any problem do not hesitate to address the Chamber if you cannot resolve it yourself. Then, I would like to move on with the following element of the trial preparation in the pre-trial phase, and I am talking about agreed facts. The Chamber considers that a part of an efficient pre-trial proceeding is to identify such issues that are not in dispute between the parties. Doing so at an early stage will save time and resources later on. And the Chamber expects the parties' full commitment in this respect, and it expects that discussions between the parties on this will commence immediately. The Chamber invites the parties to start any negotiations by looking at each sentence of the paragraphs 1 through 3 of the indictment which concern personal details and positions allegedly held by the accused, and identify whether there is agreement about the facts mentioned therein. I would say it's a relatively simple start. A second area could be, for example, paragraph 88, which relates to the existence of an armed conflict during events relevant to the indictment. But the parties could also start reviewing details with regard to the crime base for the purpose of identifying undisputed facts. I add to that that undisputed facts does not necessarily mean that there is still some dispute about what triggered these facts to happen, but that's separate. You can agree on facts and you can disagree on what caused these facts to come into existence. The Chamber also instructs the parties to regularly file progress reports on their meetings in this regard until the beginning of the trial. The first progress report should be filed on the 19th of September, and after that reports should be filed regularly one week before the planned 65 ter meetings. The progress reports should address which facts have been the subject of discussion and a summary of what keeps the parties apart in relation to those facts. And the progress reports will be addressed at the Rule 65 ter meetings and the following Status Conferences. And depending on the progress of the discussions between the parties, the Chamber might also organise separate out-of-court meetings to deal with these issues. I move on to the next matter that I would like to briefly raise with you, that is Rule 73 bis (D). On the 1st of June of this year, the Prosecution filed its second amended indictment, and under Rule 73 bis (D) of the rules, the Chamber may, after having heard the Prosecution, invite the Prosecution to reduce the number of counts charged in the indictment and may fix a number of crime sites or incidents comprised in the charges in respect of which evidence may be presented. The Chamber may do so following the disposal of any preliminary motions, if any, filed by the Defence. The Chamber notes already now that in the Karadzic case on the 8th of October, 2009, the Pre-Trial Chamber accepted the Prosecution's proposals to remove a number of municipalities and a number of incidents from the indictment. Three of the municipalities were cut from count 3, persecution, in the Karadzic case, being Bosanska Krupa, Kalinovik, and Kotor Varos -- no, I make a mistake. Three of the municipalities that were cut from the Karadzic case still remain now in the Mladic indictment, as do a number of incidents listed in schedules A, B, C, D, and E, and G. Considering the similarities between the Karadzic case and the Mladic case, the Chamber would expect the Prosecution to address, in its Rule 73 bis (D) submissions, why municipalities and incidents cut from the Karadzic case remain in the Mladic indictment. The Prosecution should expect the invitation pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D) towards the second half of November of this year. I move on to adjudicated facts. The Chamber expects the parties to file any motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts, that is by the Prosecution or Defence, during the pre-trial proceedings. By deciding on such a motion early on, this will allow the Prosecution to take the facts into account when compiling its 65 ter submissions, and in particular its witness list. The Chamber does not expect the parties to file such a motion before dealing with preliminary motions and any decision pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D). Nevertheless, the parties are instructed, in particular the Prosecution, to start the preparations for any such motion as soon as possible and be ready for filing in December of this year. The Chamber does understand that these preparations may be affected by the parties' discussions on agreed facts. I move to other pending issues. On the 31st of May, 2011, Radovan Karadzic filed a motion seeking access to confidential material in this case. The Prosecution responded on the 22nd of June, 2011. Also duty counsel responded explaining that he was not in a position to comment since disclosure had not been completed at that time. Now, permanent counsel is appointed and disclosure has been completed and, in the present circumstances, the Chamber instructs the Defence to respond to the motion filed by Mr. Karadzic by the 8th of September 2011, being two weeks from today. I have addressed all the matters which I had on my agenda, and I would like to invite the parties to address the Chamber on any issue they would like to raise. Prosecution first. Mr. McCloskey, any matters you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think we are in good shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any matter you would like to raise, already to inform Mr. Mladic that if there is any matter he would like to raise, he will have an opportunity to do so. But first, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you covered everything we discussed in the 65 ter meeting, so we don't have anything new. I will ask my client if he wants to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Mr. Mladic has not attended the 65 ter meeting, so if you would like to take instructions or see whether there are any instructions to be taken, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Mladic said if you are interested you can -- he can explain his health problems right now, but it should be probably dealt in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would -- if Mr. Mladic would like to raise his condition, his physical condition, his health, he's -- if he would prefer to do that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will do that in private session. Madam Registrar, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I referred to a few matters which were raised by Mr. Mladic; that is, that he would prefer that handcuffs and belt would be taken off. That is on the record. It will be considered by those responsible for it. And, Mr. Mladic, then, I have to explain you one thing, that security, within the premises of this Tribunal and within the UNDU is the responsibility of the Registry; however, transportation between the Detention Unit and the premises of the Tribunal here are not the responsibility of the Registry but are the responsibility of the Dutch authorities. Your observations will be conveyed to both of them. Then, is there any further matter? I am looking at the Prosecution, I am looking at you, Mr. Lukic, we have heard from Mr. Mladic who has no further matters to raise. This then concludes -- let me see. Yes. This concludes this Status Conference. I earlier announced that the Chamber will issue a scheduling order in due course, but I already can inform you now that the next Status Conference will be held on the 6th of October, 2011, and the next Rule 65 ter meeting will be held on the 3rd of October of this year. We therefore adjourn until the 6th of October 2011, half past 2.00 in the afternoon in this same courtroom, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3.23 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of October, 2011, at 2.30 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
